title: Gibbs Sampling Explained
excerpt: An algorithm to draw samples from a complex, multi-dimensional probability distribution when direct sampling is difficult, by breaking the problem down into a sequence of simpler, one-dimensional conditional distributions.
author: Somesh Chatterjee
rawContent:
# Gibbs Sampling Explained **Gibbs sampling** is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm used to draw samples from a complex, multi-dimensional probability distribution when direct sampling is difficult, by breaking the problem down into a sequence of simpler, one-dimensional conditional distributions. --- ## 1. The Core Problem & Intuition Suppose you have a joint probability distribution over multiple variables, $P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)$, and you want to generate random samples from it (for example, to estimate expected values or marginal distributions in Bayesian inference). * **The Problem:** Sampling from $P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)$ all at once is often mathematically intractable because normalizing constants (integrals over high-dimensional spaces) are impossible to compute. * **The Gibbs Solution:** Even if the joint distribution is hard to sample, the **full conditional distributions**—the distribution of one variable given fixed values for all the others, written as $P(X_i \mid X_{-i})$—are often easy to sample from. Instead of jumping straight to a point in $n$-dimensional space, Gibbs sampling takes coordinate-wise steps, updating one variable at a time while holding the others constant. ```mermaid graph LR A["Hard Problem:
Sample Jointly from
P(X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ)"] -->|Gibbs Decomposition| B["Easy Sub-problems:
Sample Conditionally"] B --> C["P(X₁ | X₂, ..., Xₙ)"] B --> D["P(X₂ | X₁, ..., Xₙ)"] B --> E["P(Xₙ | X₁, ..., Xₙ₋₁)"] C & D & E -->|Repeat in a Loop| F["Converges to Target
Joint Distribution"] ``` --- ## 2. How the Algorithm Works Let's trace a simple 2-variable case, $P(X, Y)$, to see the exact mechanics. 1. **Initialize:** Pick arbitrary starting values $(x^{(0)}, y^{(0)})$. 2. **Iterate:** For each step $t = 1, 2, \dots, T$: * Sample a new value for $X$ conditioned on the *current* value of $Y$: $$x^{(t)} \sim P(X \mid Y = y^{(t-1)})$$ * Sample a new value for $Y$ conditioned on the *newly updated* value of $X$: $$y^{(t)} \sim P(Y \mid X = x^{(t)})$$ 3. **Collect:** Save the pair $(x^{(t)}, y^{(t)})$ as a sample and repeat. Notice that in step 2b, $Y$ immediately uses the brand-new $x^{(t)}$, not $x^{(t-1)}$. ```mermaid flowchart TD Start(["Start: Initialize (x⁰, y⁰)"]) --> Step1["Set iteration t = 1"] Step1 --> SampleX["Sample x⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(X | Y = y⁽ᵗ⁻¹⁾)"] SampleX --> SampleY["Sample y⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(Y | X = x⁽ᵗ⁾)"] SampleY --> Store["Record sample (x⁽ᵗ⁾, y⁽ᵗ⁾)"] Store --> Check{"t == Max Iterations?"} Check -- No --> Inc["t = t + 1"] Inc --> SampleX Check -- Yes --> End(["End: Return Sample Chain"]) ``` --- ## 3. The State-Space Trajectory (Orthogonal Moves) Because Gibbs sampling updates one variable at a time, its movement through the probability space looks like a staircase or a Manhattan grid—it only ever moves parallel to the coordinate axes. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant State as Current State (X, Y) participant CondX as Conditional P(X | Y) participant CondY as Conditional P(Y | X) Note over State: Starts at (x⁰, y⁰) State->>CondX: Fix Y = y⁰ CondX-->>State: Moves horizontally to (x¹, y⁰) State->>CondY: Fix X = x¹ CondY-->>State: Moves vertically to (x¹, y¹) State->>CondX: Fix Y = y¹ CondX-->>State: Moves horizontally to (x², y¹) State->>CondY: Fix X = x² CondY-->>State: Moves vertically to (x², y²) ``` --- ## 4. Practical Considerations in MCMC To get reliable results from a Gibbs sampler, you cannot just blindly use every number it spits out. Two standard post-processing steps are required: 1. **Burn-in Period:** Because you start at an arbitrary guess $(x^{(0)}, y^{(0)})$, the early samples might be in a very low-probability region far from the true distribution. You discard the first $B$ samples (e.g., the first 1,000 iterations) to give the Markov chain time to "forget" its starting point and reach its stationary distribution. 2. **Thinning (Autocorrelation):** Because $(x^{(t)}, y^{(t)})$ is directly generated from $(x^{(t-1)}, y^{(t-1)})$, consecutive samples are correlated, not strictly independent. Sometimes practitioners keep only every $k$-th sample (thinning) if memory is constrained, though modern practice often keeps all post-burn-in samples and accounts for autocorrelation when computing standard errors. ```mermaid gantt title Lifecycle of a Gibbs Sampling Chain dateFormat X axisFormat %s section Phase 1 Burn-in (Discarded) :crit, 0, 200 section Phase 2 Stationary Sampling (Kept) :active, 200, 1000 ``` --- ## 5. End-to-End Architecture Putting all components together—decomposition, initialization, sequential sweeps, burn-in filtering, and posterior estimation: ```mermaid flowchart TD %% Styling classDef startend fill:#1e293b,stroke:#0f172a,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px classDef process fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:1.5px classDef update fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#22c55e,color:#14532d,stroke-width:1.5px classDef decision fill:#fefce8,stroke:#eab308,color:#713f12,stroke-width:1.5px classDef discard fill:#fef2f2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:1.5px Start(["Target Joint Distribution
P(X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ)
(Intractable to sample directly)"]):::startend Decomp["1. Decompose into Full Conditionals
Derive P(Xᵢ | X₋ᵢ) for each variable i = 1...n"]:::process Init["2. Initialize State
Pick arbitrary starting point:
X⁽⁰⁾ = (x₁⁽⁰⁾, x₂⁽⁰⁾, ..., xₙ⁽⁰⁾)
Set iteration t = 1"]:::process subgraph Loop ["3. Coordinate-Wise Sweep (Iteration t)"] direction TB U1["Sample x₁⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(X₁ | x₂⁽ᵗ⁻¹⁾, ..., xₙ⁽ᵗ⁻¹⁾)"]:::update U2["Sample x₂⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(X₂ | x₁⁽ᵗ⁾, x₃⁽ᵗ⁻¹⁾, ..., xₙ⁽ᵗ⁻¹⁾)"]:::update Dots["... update remaining variables sequentially ..."]:::update Un["Sample xₙ⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(Xₙ | x₁⁽ᵗ⁾, ..., xₙ₋₁⁽ᵗ⁾)"]:::update U1 --> U2 --> Dots --> Un end BurnCheck{"4. Burn-in Check
Is t ≤ Burn-in (B)?"}:::decision Discard["Discard Sample X⁽ᵗ⁾
Chain is still converging to
stationary distribution"]:::discard Keep["Store Sample X⁽ᵗ⁾
Add to valid posterior samples"]:::process MaxCheck{"5. Stopping Criterion
Is t == Total Iterations (T)?"}:::decision Inc["Increment t = t + 1"]:::process End(["Output Empirical Distribution
Use stored samples {X⁽ᴮ⁺¹⁾, ..., X⁽ᵀ⁾}
to estimate expectations & marginals"]):::startend %% Connections Start --> Decomp --> Init --> U1 Un --> BurnCheck BurnCheck -- "Yes (Warm-up)" --> Discard --> MaxCheck BurnCheck -- "No (Converged)" --> Keep --> MaxCheck MaxCheck -- "No" --> Inc --> U1 MaxCheck -- "Yes" --> End ``` --- ## 6. Strengths vs. Limitations | Feature | Strengths | Limitations | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Tuning** | **Zero hyperparameters.** Unlike Metropolis-Hastings, you don't need to tune a proposal step size; every proposed sample is accepted (acceptance rate = 100%). | **Requires closed-form conditionals.** You must be able to mathematically derive and sample from every $P(X_i \mid X_{-i})$. | | **High Dimensions** | Breaks a massive $N$-dimensional integral into $N$ simple 1D updates. | **Struggles with high correlation.** If $X$ and $Y$ are strongly correlated (a narrow diagonal ridge), taking only horizontal/vertical steps causes the sampler to crawl very slowly. | --- ## 7. Relationship to Metropolis-Hastings Gibbs sampling is actually a **special case of the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm**. In MH, you propose a move and accept or reject it based on an acceptance probability $\alpha$. If you choose the full conditional distribution $P(X_i \mid X_{-i})$ as your MH proposal distribution, the math simplifies so that $\alpha = 1$ every single time. ```mermaid graph TD MCMC["MCMC Methods
(Markov Chain Monte Carlo)"] --> MH["Metropolis-Hastings
(Propose & Accept/Reject)"] MCMC --> HMC["Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
(Uses gradients / physics)"] MH -->|Special Case: Proposal = Full Conditional
Acceptance Rate = 100%| Gibbs["Gibbs Sampling"] Gibbs --> Blocked["Blocked Gibbs
(Updates groups of variables together)"] Gibbs --> Collapsed["Collapsed Gibbs
(Integrates out certain variables analytically)"] ``` ## Simple Numerical Example: Weather & Ice Cream Sales Imagine a small town where two things happen each day: 1. **Weather (W):** Either **Sunny (S)** or **Rainy (R)**. 2. **Ice Cream Shop (C):** Either **Busy (B)** or **Quiet (Q)**. Suppose we know the joint probabilities of all 4 combinations over a year: | | **Busy (B)** | **Quiet (Q)** | **Total Weather** | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Sunny (S)** | **0.50** (50%) | **0.10** (10%) | 0.60 (60%) | | **Rainy (R)** | **0.05** (5%) | **0.35** (35%) | 0.40 (40%) | | **Total Shop** | 0.55 (55%) | 0.45 (45%) | **1.00** | **Goal:** Generate random simulated days $(W, C)$ that match this table by updating one variable at a time. --- ### Step 1: Find the 4 Simple Conditional Rules (Just Ratios!) To sample one variable given the other, simply look at that row or column and take the ratio: 1. **If it is Sunny ($W = S$):** The row is `0.50` Busy vs. `0.10` Quiet (a 5-to-1 ratio). * $P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Sunny}) = \frac{0.50}{0.50 + 0.10} = \frac{5}{6} \approx \mathbf{83\%}$ * $P(\text{Quiet} \mid \text{Sunny}) = \frac{1}{6} \approx \mathbf{17\%}$ 2. **If it is Rainy ($W = R$):** The row is `0.05` Busy vs. `0.35` Quiet (a 1-to-7 ratio). * $P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Rainy}) = \frac{0.05}{0.05 + 0.35} = \frac{1}{8} = \mathbf{12.5\%}$ * $P(\text{Quiet} \mid \text{Rainy}) = \frac{7}{8} = \mathbf{87.5\%}$ 3. **If the shop is Busy ($C = B$):** The column is `0.50` Sunny vs. `0.05` Rainy (a 10-to-1 ratio). * $P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Busy}) = \frac{0.50}{0.50 + 0.05} = \frac{10}{11} \approx \mathbf{91\%}$ * $P(\text{Rainy} \mid \text{Busy}) = \frac{1}{11} \approx \mathbf{9\%}$ 4. **If the shop is Quiet ($C = Q$):** The column is `0.10` Sunny vs. `0.35` Rainy (a 2-to-7 ratio). * $P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Quiet}) = \frac{0.10}{0.10 + 0.35} = \frac{2}{9} \approx \mathbf{22\%}$ * $P(\text{Rainy} \mid \text{Quiet}) = \frac{7}{9} \approx \mathbf{78\%}$ --- ### Step 2: Simulate 3 Days by Drawing Random Numbers (1–100) Let's start with an unlikely combination: **Day 0 = (Rainy, Busy)**. #### **Day 1** 1. **Update Weather (given Shop = Busy):** * Rule 3 says there is a **91% chance of Sunny** and **9% chance of Rainy**. * Draw a random number from 1 to 100 and get `34` ($\le 91$). * New Weather = **Sunny**. 2. **Update Shop (given the new Weather = Sunny):** * Rule 1 says there is an **83% chance of Busy** and **17% chance of Quiet**. * Draw a random number from 1 to 100 and get `62` ($\le 83$). * New Shop = **Busy**. * **Simulated Day 1:** **(Sunny, Busy)** #### **Day 2** 1. **Update Weather (given Shop = Busy):** * Rule 3: **91% Sunny** vs. **9% Rainy**. * Random draw = `95` ($> 91$). * New Weather = **Rainy**. 2. **Update Shop (given the new Weather = Rainy):** * Rule 2 says there is a **12.5% chance of Busy** and **87.5% chance of Quiet**. * Random draw = `48` ($> 12.5$). * New Shop = **Quiet**. * **Simulated Day 2:** **(Rainy, Quiet)** #### **Day 3** 1. **Update Weather (given Shop = Quiet):** * Rule 4: **22% Sunny** vs. **78% Rainy**. * Random draw = `71` ($> 22$). * New Weather = **Rainy**. 2. **Update Shop (given Weather = Rainy):** * Rule 2: **12.5% Busy** vs. **87.5% Quiet**. * Random draw = `19` ($> 12.5$). * New Shop = **Quiet**. * **Simulated Day 3:** **(Rainy, Quiet)** --- ### Step 3: Visual Flow of the 3 Days ```mermaid flowchart LR D0["Day 0 (Start)
(Rainy, Busy)"] -->|"Shop = Busy
(91% Sunny)"| D0_5["(Sunny, Busy)"] D0_5 -->|"Weather = Sunny
(83% Busy)"| D1["Day 1
(Sunny, Busy)"] D1 -->|"Shop = Busy
(9% Rainy)"| D1_5["(Rainy, Busy)"] D1_5 -->|"Weather = Rainy
(87.5% Quiet)"| D2["Day 2
(Rainy, Quiet)"] D2 -->|"Shop = Quiet
(78% Rainy)"| D2_5["(Rainy, Quiet)"] D2_5 -->|"Weather = Rainy
(87.5% Quiet)"| D3["Day 3
(Rainy, Quiet)"] ``` ### Why This Works If you repeat this game 10,000 times and count your simulated days: * About **5,000 days (50%)** will be *(Sunny, Busy)* * About **1,000 days (10%)** will be *(Sunny, Quiet)* * About **500 days (5%)** will be *(Rainy, Busy)* * About **3,500 days (35%)** will be *(Rainy, Quiet)* Even though you only ever flipped weighted coins for **one variable at a time**, the pairs naturally settle into the exact proportions of the original 2D table. ## How Gibbs Sampling Solves a Problem When the Table Isn't Known Upfront When the probability table is unknown upfront, **Gibbs sampling solves the inverse problem (Bayesian inference) by alternating between guessing the missing labels for your data and updating the unknown probabilities based on those guesses.** Instead of knowing the probabilities and generating data, you have **real-world data with missing information** (latent variables) and **unknown rules** (parameters), and Gibbs sampling discovers both simultaneously. --- ### 1. The Real-World Problem: Hidden Causes Imagine you are the manager of a newly opened ice cream shop, and you don't know the town's probability table yet. You have 100 days of sales logs (**Busy** or **Quiet**), and you know there are two hidden weather patterns (**Sunny** or **Rainy**), *but your historical log forgot to record the weather!* You have two unknowns that depend on each other: 1. **Missing Labels ($Z$):** Was Day 1 Sunny or Rainy? What about Day 2? 2. **Unknown Probabilities ($\theta$):** What is the true chance of being Busy on a Sunny day vs. a Rainy day? ```mermaid graph LR Data["Observed Data (Known)
100 days of Shop Logs:
[Busy, Busy, Quiet, ...]"] Labels["Missing Labels (Unknown)
Weather on each day:
[Sunny?, Rainy?, ...]"] Params["Probability Table (Unknown)
P(Busy | Sunny) = ?
P(Busy | Rainy) = ?"] Labels <-->|"Chicken-and-Egg Loop"| Params Data --> Labels Data --> Params ``` * If you knew the **Probability Table**, you could easily guess the **Weather** for each day. * If you knew the **Weather** for each day, you could easily count the rows and calculate the **Probability Table**. Gibbs sampling breaks this chicken-and-egg deadlock by starting with a random guess and alternating between the two. --- ### 2. How Gibbs Sampling Discovers the Table #### **Step 0: Random Initialization** Since you know nothing, flip a fair coin to randomly assign **Sunny** or **Rainy** to every single day in your 100-day log. (At first, these labels are pure noise.) #### **Step 1: Sample the Unknown Probabilities ($\theta \mid \text{Data}, Z$)** Pretend your current weather labels are true, and simply **count**: * Out of the days currently labeled *Sunny*, say 32 were *Busy* and 18 were *Quiet*. * Instead of taking a rigid ratio, Gibbs sampling draws a random probability from a **Beta distribution** centered around that ratio (e.g., $\text{Beta}(32+1, 18+1)$), which might give **$P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Sunny}) = 65\%$**. * Do the same for *Rainy* days, say giving **$P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Rainy}) = 20\%$**. #### **Step 2: Re-Sample the Missing Labels ($Z \mid \text{Data}, \theta$)** Now use those newly updated probabilities to re-guess the weather for each day one by one using **Bayes' Rule**: * Look at **Day 1**, where the shop was **Busy**. * Since *Busy* happens **65%** of the time on Sunny days vs. only **20%** on Rainy days, Day 1 is much more likely to have been Sunny ($\frac{65}{65+20} \approx \mathbf{76\%}$ chance of Sunny). * Flip a weighted coin (76% Sunny / 24% Rainy) to assign a fresh weather label to Day 1. Repeat for all 100 days. #### **Step 3: Repeat 1,000 Times** Every time you repeat Steps 1 and 2, the noise cancels out: * Days that were *Busy* cluster together under one label, pushing its Busy probability up toward the true **83%**. * Days that were *Quiet* cluster together under the other label, pushing its Busy probability down toward the true **12.5%**. ```mermaid flowchart TD Init["0. Random Guess
Assign random Sunny/Rainy labels
to all 100 days of sales logs"] --> Count subgraph Sweep ["Gibbs Sampling Iteration (Repeat 1,000x)"] Count["1. Update Probability Table
Count Busy vs. Quiet days inside each group
Sample new probabilities from Beta distributions"] Relabel["2. Re-label Every Day
Use new probabilities + Bayes' Rule
to flip weighted coins for each day's weather"] Count --> Relabel end Relabel --> Check{"Converged?"} Check -- No --> Count Check -- Yes --> Output["Output Discovered Table
Average the sampled probability tables
after burn-in (e.g., 83% vs 12.5%)"] ``` --- ### 3. Why This Is Used Everywhere in AI & Data Science This exact pattern—**inferring unknown labels and unknown probabilities from raw data**—is how real-world machine learning models work when the ground truth isn't given: | Application | Observed Data (Known) | Missing Labels ($Z$) | Unknown Table ($\theta$) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Topic Modeling (LDA)** | Thousands of news articles | Which topic each word belongs to | Word probabilities per topic (e.g., *"goal"* = 5% in Sports) | | **Customer Segmentation** | Purchase histories | Which persona each shopper belongs to | Buying habits of each customer segment | | **Genetics / Population Structure** | DNA sequences of individuals | Ancestral population of each gene | Allele frequencies in each ancestral group |

Gibbs Sampling Explained

Gibbs sampling is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm used to draw samples from a complex, multi-dimensional probability distribution when direct sampling is difficult, by breaking the problem down into a sequence of simpler, one-dimensional conditional distributions.

1. The Core Problem & Intuition

Suppose you have a joint probability distribution over multiple variables, P(X1,X2,…,Xn)P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)P(X1​,X2​,…,Xn​), and you want to generate random samples from it (for example, to estimate expected values or marginal distributions in Bayesian inference).

  • The Problem: Sampling from P(X1,X2,…,Xn)P(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)P(X1​,X2​,…,Xn​) all at once is often mathematically intractable because normalizing constants (integrals over high-dimensional spaces) are impossible to compute.
  • The Gibbs Solution: Even if the joint distribution is hard to sample, the full conditional distributions—the distribution of one variable given fixed values for all the others, written as P(Xi∣X−i)P(X_i \mid X_{-i})P(Xi​∣X−i​)—are often easy to sample from.

Instead of jumping straight to a point in nnn-dimensional space, Gibbs sampling takes coordinate-wise steps, updating one variable at a time while holding the others constant.

graph LR
    A["Hard Problem:<br>Sample Jointly from<br>P(X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ)"] -->|Gibbs Decomposition| B["Easy Sub-problems:<br>Sample Conditionally"]
    B --> C["P(X₁ | X₂, ..., Xₙ)"]
    B --> D["P(X₂ | X₁, ..., Xₙ)"]
    B --> E["P(Xₙ | X₁, ..., Xₙ₋₁)"]
    C & D & E -->|Repeat in a Loop| F["Converges to Target<br>Joint Distribution"]

2. How the Algorithm Works

Let's trace a simple 2-variable case, P(X,Y)P(X, Y)P(X,Y), to see the exact mechanics.

  1. Initialize: Pick arbitrary starting values (x(0),y(0))(x^{(0)}, y^{(0)})(x(0),y(0)).
  2. Iterate: For each step t=1,2,…,Tt = 1, 2, \dots, Tt=1,2,…,T:
    • Sample a new value for XXX conditioned on the current value of YYY: x(t)∼P(X∣Y=y(t−1))x^{(t)} \sim P(X \mid Y = y^{(t-1)})x(t)∼P(X∣Y=y(t−1))
    • Sample a new value for YYY conditioned on the newly updated value of XXX: y(t)∼P(Y∣X=x(t))y^{(t)} \sim P(Y \mid X = x^{(t)})y(t)∼P(Y∣X=x(t))
  3. Collect: Save the pair (x(t),y(t))(x^{(t)}, y^{(t)})(x(t),y(t)) as a sample and repeat.

Notice that in step 2b, YYY immediately uses the brand-new x(t)x^{(t)}x(t), not x(t−1)x^{(t-1)}x(t−1).

    SampleX --> SampleY["Sample y⁽ᵗ⁾ ~ P(Y | X = x⁽ᵗ⁾)"]
    SampleY --> Store["Record sample (x⁽ᵗ⁾, y⁽ᵗ⁾)"]
    Store --> Check{"t == Max Iterations?"}
    Check -- No --> Inc["t = t + 1"]
    Inc --> SampleX
    Check -- Yes --> End(["End: Return Sample Chain"])

3. The State-Space Trajectory (Orthogonal Moves)

Because Gibbs sampling updates one variable at a time, its movement through the probability space looks like a staircase or a Manhattan grid—it only ever moves parallel to the coordinate axes.

4. Practical Considerations in MCMC

To get reliable results from a Gibbs sampler, you cannot just blindly use every number it spits out. Two standard post-processing steps are required:

  1. Burn-in Period: Because you start at an arbitrary guess (x(0),y(0))(x^{(0)}, y^{(0)})(x(0),y(0)), the early samples might be in a very low-probability region far from the true distribution. You discard the first BBB samples (e.g., the first 1,000 iterations) to give the Markov chain time to "forget" its starting point and reach its stationary distribution.
  2. Thinning (Autocorrelation): Because (x(t),y(t))(x^{(t)}, y^{(t)})(x(t),y(t)) is directly generated from (x(t−1),y(t−1))(x^{(t-1)}, y^{(t-1)})(x(t−1),y(t−1)), consecutive samples are correlated, not strictly independent. Sometimes practitioners keep only every kkk-th sample (thinning) if memory is constrained, though modern practice often keeps all post-burn-in samples and accounts for autocorrelation when computing standard errors.

Tuning Zero hyperparameters. Unlike Metropolis-Hastings, you don't need to tune a proposal step size; every proposed sample is accepted (acceptance rate = 100%). Requires closed-form conditionals. You must be able to mathematically derive and sample from every P(Xi∣X−i)P(X_i \mid X_{-i})P(Xi​∣X−i​).
High Dimensions Breaks a massive NNN-dimensional integral into NNN simple 1D updates. Struggles with high correlation. If XXX and YYY are strongly correlated (a narrow diagonal ridge), taking only horizontal/vertical steps causes the sampler to crawl very slowly.

7. Relationship to Metropolis-Hastings

Gibbs sampling is actually a special case of the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm. In MH, you propose a move and accept or reject it based on an acceptance probability α\alphaα. If you choose the full conditional distribution P(Xi∣X−i)P(X_i \mid X_{-i})P(Xi​∣X−i​) as your MH proposal distribution, the math simplifies so that α=1\alpha = 1α=1 every single time.

Simple Numerical Example: Weather & Ice Cream Sales

Imagine a small town where two things happen each day:

  1. Weather (W): Either Sunny (S) or Rainy (R).
  2. Ice Cream Shop (C): Either Busy (B) or Quiet (Q).

Suppose we know the joint probabilities of all 4 combinations over a year:

Goal: Generate random simulated days (W,C)(W, C)(W,C) that match this table by updating one variable at a time.

Step 1: Find the 4 Simple Conditional Rules (Just Ratios!)

To sample one variable given the other, simply look at that row or column and take the ratio:

  1. If it is Sunny (W=SW = SW=S): The row is 0.50 Busy vs. 0.10 Quiet (a 5-to-1 ratio).

Why This Works

If you repeat this game 10,000 times and count your simulated days:

  • About 5,000 days (50%) will be (Sunny, Busy)
  • About 1,000 days (10%) will be (Sunny, Quiet)
  • About 500 days (5%) will be (Rainy, Busy)
  • About 3,500 days (35%) will be (Rainy, Quiet)

Even though you only ever flipped weighted coins for one variable at a time, the pairs naturally settle into the exact proportions of the original 2D table.

How Gibbs Sampling Solves a Problem When the Table Isn't Known Upfront

When the probability table is unknown upfront, Gibbs sampling solves the inverse problem (Bayesian inference) by alternating between guessing the missing labels for your data and updating the unknown probabilities based on those guesses.

Instead of knowing the probabilities and generating data, you have real-world data with missing information (latent variables) and unknown rules (parameters), and Gibbs sampling discovers both simultaneously.

1. The Real-World Problem: Hidden Causes

Imagine you are the manager of a newly opened ice cream shop, and you don't know the town's probability table yet. You have 100 days of sales logs (Busy or Quiet), and you know there are two hidden weather patterns (Sunny or Rainy), but your historical log forgot to record the weather!

You have two unknowns that depend on each other:

  1. Missing Labels (ZZZ): Was Day 1 Sunny or Rainy? What about Day 2?
  2. Unknown Probabilities (θ\thetaθ): What is the true chance of being Busy on a Sunny day vs. a Rainy day?

  • If you knew the Probability Table, you could easily guess the Weather for each day.
  • If you knew the Weather for each day, you could easily count the rows and calculate the Probability Table.

Gibbs sampling breaks this chicken-and-egg deadlock by starting with a random guess and alternating between the two.

2. How Gibbs Sampling Discovers the Table

Step 0: Random Initialization

Since you know nothing, flip a fair coin to randomly assign Sunny or Rainy to every single day in your 100-day log. (At first, these labels are pure noise.)

Step 1: Sample the Unknown Probabilities (θ∣Data,Z\theta \mid \text{Data}, Zθ∣Data,Z)

Pretend your current weather labels are true, and simply count:

  • Out of the days currently labeled Sunny, say 32 were Busy and 18 were Quiet.
  • Instead of taking a rigid ratio, Gibbs sampling draws a random probability from a Beta distribution centered around that ratio (e.g., Beta(32+1,18+1)\text{Beta}(32+1, 18+1)Beta(32+1,18+1)), which might give P(Busy∣Sunny)=65%P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Sunny}) = 65\%P(Busy∣Sunny)=65%.
  • Do the same for Rainy days, say giving P(Busy∣Rainy)=20%P(\text{Busy} \mid \text{Rainy}) = 20\%P(Busy∣Rainy)=20%.

Step 2: Re-Sample the Missing Labels (Z∣Data,θZ \mid \text{Data}, \thetaZ∣Data,θ)

Now use those newly updated probabilities to re-guess the weather for each day one by one using Bayes' Rule:

  • Look at Day 1, where the shop was Busy.
  • Since Busy happens 65% of the time on Sunny days vs. only 20% on Rainy days, Day 1 is much more likely to have been Sunny (6565+20≈76%\frac{65}{65+20} \approx \mathbf{76\%}65+2065​≈76% chance of Sunny).
  • Flip a weighted coin (76% Sunny / 24% Rainy) to assign a fresh weather label to Day 1. Repeat for all 100 days.

Step 3: Repeat 1,000 Times

Every time you repeat Steps 1 and 2, the noise cancels out:

  • Days that were Busy cluster together under one label, pushing its Busy probability up toward the true 83%.
  • Days that were Quiet cluster together under the other label, pushing its Busy probability down toward the true 12.5%.

3. Why This Is Used Everywhere in AI & Data Science

This exact pattern—inferring unknown labels and unknown probabilities from raw data—is how real-world machine learning models work when the ground truth isn't given:
